papers_read.title_as_printed: Identifying and Predicting Cognitive Decline Using Multi-Modal Sensor Data and Machine Learning Approach (Joshi et al., Research Square preprint, 2025)
AI-Driven Prediction of Possible Mild Cognitive Impairment Using the Oculo-Cognitive Addition Test (OCAT) (Pradhan et al., Brain Sci. 2026, 16, 70)

what_each_reports.P-331: 118 Nebraska drivers (72 cognitively impaired: 64 MCI + 8 dementia, clinician-adjudicated per NIA-AA 2018; 46 healthy aging). XGBoost on 3 months of naturalistic driving + actigraphy sleep + demographics, nested CV with LOSO outer loop: accuracy 68.64%, precision 73.97%, recall 75.00%, F1 74.48%.
what_each_reports.P-282: 206 Mayo Clinic Arizona APOE-cohort participants (166 CN, 40 'possible MCI' defined as Mattis DRS < 140, including mild dementia). Logistic regression on OCAT eye-movement + time features + age, 80/20 stratified split (test n=42: 31 CN, 11 PMCI), SMOTE on training: Table 5 LR-SMOTE accuracy 0.94 [0.88-0.98] (DT 0.5), 0.93 (DT 0.45); the abstract states accuracy 0.97. No external validation.

quantity_a: Subject-level accuracy for classifying clinician-diagnosed MCI or dementia vs healthy aging in community drivers from passive driving, sleep and demographic data, leave-one-subject-out CV
quantity_b: Hold-out accuracy for classifying a psychometric threshold (DRS score < 140, 'possible MCI', explicitly an early-risk label) vs DRS >= 140 in neurology-clinic cohort participants from a one-minute eye-tracked mental-addition task, 42-person test set
incompatible_if_same: Would appear incompatible numerically (68.64% vs 0.94), but P-282's majority-class baseline on its test set is 31/42 = 74% vs P-331's 61%, and the endpoints differ in kind, so the gap is not interpretable as a disagreement.

gates.task: mismatch in substance: both detection tasks, but P-331's target is clinician-adjudicated MCI/dementia and P-282's target is a DRS cut-off that the authors say captures 'early cognitive risk rather than established impairment'; registry codes P-331 as T2 while the record says T1
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: Nebraska community driver sample vs Mayo Clinic Arizona APOE cohort; the record's dataset_equal 'Yes' rests on both registry rows reading 'not reported'
gates.validation_tier: match: both internal only (LOSO CV vs single stratified hold-out)
gates.modality_family: mismatch in substance: both coded digital_behaviour, but passive naturalistic driving + wrist actigraphy vs active task-based eye tracking during mental arithmetic

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: accuracy in both, but against different reference standards (clinical diagnosis vs DRS < 140) and different class balance
performance_validity: flag applies to the headline figure: P-282's abstract reports accuracy 0.97 on internal validation with a 42-person test set and no external cohort, which meets the Section 2 exclusion; even its table value (0.94) is internal-only on n=42
independence: Distinct studies, cohorts and author groups
grounds: P-282's outcome is a DRS score below 140, which its authors say indicates early cognitive risk rather than established MCI, while P-331's outcome is clinician-adjudicated MCI or dementia.

The input modalities differ in kind (passive driving and sleep vs eye tracking during a mental-addition task) and the cohorts differ, so the dataset-family and modality gates fail with no waiver on record.

P-282's headline accuracy of 0.97 is internal validation on a 42-person test set with no external cohort, so the performance-validity exclusion would bar a performance comparison even if the quantities matched.

evidence_quotes.quote: the model 6 integrating demographics, driving performance, driving life-space, and sleep data achieved the highest accuracy (68.64%), precision (73.97%), and F1-score (74.48%).
Participants with cognitive decline but without substantial functional impairments were classified as having MCI. Those who showed both cognitive and functional decline were classified as dementia.
As per the clinical standards, participants with a DRS score of 140 or above were labeled as CN, and those with less than 140 scores were labeled as PMCI [38].
it likely captures earlier or subtler impairment rather than definitive MCI and may limit direct comparability with studies using lower, more traditional cutoffs (e.g., 123) [9].
LR models achieved the highest performance using the combined time and eye movement features, with an accuracy of 0.97, recall of 0.91, and an AUPRC of 0.95.
However, model development and evaluation were conducted within a single cohort, and the absence of external validation limits generalizability.

record_defects: dataset_equal 'Yes' is wrong: the two studies use unrelated cohorts (Nebraska drivers vs Mayo Clinic Arizona APOE cohort); both registry rows merely say 'not reported'.
claim_b 'Acc 0.97' is the abstract figure; P-282's own Table 5 gives 0.94 [0.88-0.98] for the best LR model, an internal inconsistency in the source that the record does not note.
claim_a labels P-331 as T1 whereas the registry codes it T2.

resolution_note's rejection reason ('Same architecture family (A1_classical)') is not a ground under the rule; the real grounds are endpoint, cohort and modality differences and the performance-validity exclusion.
what_would_change_the_verdict: Nothing within these two papers: a comparison would need both to use the same reference standard (clinical MCI diagnosis) in comparable cohorts with externally validated, prevalence-robust metrics.
